https://bnn-news.com/bnn-in-focus-politi.text: Photo: LETA/BNN collage/AI Advertisements Paradoxically, the National Alliance’s (NA) biggest problem at the moment is that many of the issues the party has championed in Latvian politics for years – the transition to Latvian as the language of education and the public sphere, a much tougher stance towards Russia, higher defence spending, the removal of the Soviet legacy and an increasingly cautious approach to immigration – are no longer exclusively NA issues. To varying degrees, they have also been adopted by other political forces. Although the ratings suggest that some National Alliance voters have moved to other political forces – from 9.4% in the 14th Saeima election to 4.5% in the SKDS poll this August – the party still has its own loyal voters, some of whom have supported it since the days of the slogan “Latvian, don’t give up!” For years, NA sought to make Latvian politics more Latvian-oriented, more firmly opposed to Russia, tougher on security issues and more cautious towards immigration. These issues were important enough to the party’s voters for them to cast their ballots specifically for the nationalists. Traditionally, NA has been a political force with a “core electorate”. Yet, as the decline in its ratings suggests, part of that electorate has now become less loyal to the party. Why? National-conservative rhetoric centred on sovereignty, family values and strict migration policies is now being offered in various combinations by several other candidate lists. This means that voters who consider these values important no longer have to choose NA. The party must therefore compete with other political forces operating in the right-wing nationalist and socially conservative political space. Advertisements Leaders of the party’s candidate lists NA is heading into the 15th Saeima election without Raivis Dzintars, a politician with whom the party had been closely associated since the establishment of the National Alliance “All for Latvia! – For Fatherland and Freedom/LNNK” in 2010. In this election, Ilze Indriksone is the party’s candidate for prime minister and heads its Riga list. Jānis Dombrava is number one in Vidzeme, Jānis Vitenbergs heads the Zemgale list, Artūrs Butāns leads the Kurzeme list, and Edmunds Teirumnieks is number one in Latgale. As Minister of Education and Science, Ilze Indriksone inherited a difficult portfolio – the issue of raising teachers’ salaries, disputes surrounding general education reform, proposals to tighten requirements for foreign students, and other challenges. Advertisements Jānis Dombrava is positioned as NA’s leading politician on migration and national security. The Ministry of the Interior regularly highlights its minister’s achievements, recalling Operation VILKATIS on the Latvia–Belarus border, expanded video surveillance capabilities for border guards, the beginning of work to introduce State Defence Service within the State Border Guard, and other measures. Vitenbergs has ministerial experience at the Ministry of Economics, the Ministry of Transport and now the Ministry of Climate and Energy. He has identified the security of energy infrastructure, readiness for the heating season and improving the business environment as his main priorities. Artūrs Butāns is one of the most visible politicians of NA’s younger generation and clearly one of the figures on whom the party is building its post-Dzintars era. Edmunds Teirumnieks, who holds a doctorate in engineering and is a professor and leading researcher at the RTU Rēzekne Academy, is more closely associated with regional development, higher education and the interests of Latgale. Advertisements Culture Minister Nauris Puntulis, who is running as number two on the Riga list, has long personified NA’s cultural policy. Ināra Mūrniece, meanwhile, who is running as number two in Vidzeme, brings the party the experience of a former Saeima Speaker and defence minister, and currently chairs the Saeima Foreign Affairs Committee. At European level, the party also still has Roberts Zīle – one of NA’s longest-serving and most internationally recognisable political figures. From ideology to social and economic issues The party promises the right to receive any service in Latvian in both the public and private sectors, greater powers for the State Language Centre and a Latvian “derussification declaration”. Advertisements In the field of security, NA proposes spending more than 5% of GDP on defence, developing Latvia’s domestic military industry, strengthening air-defence, drone and counter-drone capabilities, and increasing the number of trained reservists. Its offer to families is also quite attractive. NA promises to increase the childcare allowance to 600 euros and index it, while setting the state family benefit at 100 euros for one child, 300 euros for two children and 600 euros for three or more children. The party also promises fully state-funded healthcare for children, partial cancellation of student loans after the birth of a child, a 15,000-euro grant to reduce a mortgage for each child, and state-guaranteed housing loans for young families without a down payment. This fits well with the party’s traditional identity politics: if Latvia wants more Latvians living in Latvia, the state should provide families with as much support as possible to encourage them to have more children. Advertisements Yet no matter how attractive election promises may sound, fiscal and political reality tends to bring dreamers back down to earth after an election. First, there is a significant difference between making promises and securing the funding required to fulfil them. Parties would therefore be well advised to explain where they intend to find the money, particularly at a time when the state is simultaneously promising more funding for defence, healthcare, internal security and other sectors. Second, it should not be forgotten that political decisions are made through compromise, dictated by coalition dynamics, the aforementioned budget constraints and unforeseen crises such as the Covid pandemic or geopolitical conflicts. And finally, there are populism and bureaucracy. Family policy is unlikely to be an issue that any party would actively oppose, but no one has abolished bureaucratic foot-dragging. Advertisements The hot potato – migration Migration is the hot potato that the governing coalition is currently tossing from hand to hand, without quite knowing what to do with it during the election campaign. On the one hand, part of society demands restrictions on virtually any form of immigration and is concerned about the associated security risks. On the other hand, there is a growing demand for labour that is becoming increasingly difficult to meet without employing third-country nationals. NA’s position is aimed at reducing immigration as much as possible, while its ideological opponents on values and social policy – the Progressives – oppose a migration policy based on “prejudice, racism and fear of those who are different”. Advertisements ZZS, meanwhile, points to the need to address labour shortages in Latvia’s economy and therefore supports controlled “labour migration”. New Unity holds a similar position. It is also worth recalling that Prime Minister Andris Kulbergs of the United List blocked Interior Minister Jānis Dombrava’s migration restriction plan at a government meeting, describing it, among other things, as “political theatre” and an attempt to mislead voters. From an election campaign perspective, however, this conflict gives NA an opportunity to demonstrate that although it is part of the government, it maintains a firm position on issues that matter to the party and its voters. In other words, the old “strong backbone” meme associated with NA’s predecessor, For Fatherland and Freedom/LNNK, and its positioning as the party most ideologically consistent on national issues have not disappeared. Advertisements Strict migration controls therefore fit NA’s traditional identity. At the same time, employers’ arguments about labour shortages, universities’ interest in attracting foreign students – and their money – as well as EU legal constraints remain relevant to a significant part of society. In August, when migration had already become one of NA’s central political issues, the party’s rating in the SKDS poll fell from 5.5% to 4.5%. This alone does not prove a causal relationship between the party’s position on migration and the decline in support among potential voters. Nevertheless, there is a considerable possibility that the more moderate section of NA’s electorate has turned away from the party precisely because of its consistent strategy of restricting migration. What the ratings show Advertisements The National Alliance spent almost the entire 14th Saeima term alternating between being a governing party and an opposition force. Following the 2022 election, NA was part of Krišjānis Kariņš’ government, but after Evika Siliņa formed her government in 2023, the party moved into opposition. As a result, NA spent most of the parliamentary term outside government and was able to enjoy the politically convenient advantage of criticising virtually any government decision without having to take responsibility for it itself. This may have been one of the reasons why NA recorded some of its strongest ratings during its period in opposition – 9.9% in the December 2024 SKDS poll and, after a slight decline in March and April, 9.7% in July 2025. Advertisements Last autumn, however, NA’s ratings began to fall sharply – from 9.7% in July to 6.4% in October and 5.6% in November. The political conflict surrounding the Istanbul Convention punched a major hole in NA’s support. In an SKDS poll, 40% of NA voters said Latvia should definitely withdraw from the Convention, while another 16% said it should probably withdraw. At the same time, 22% said Latvia should definitely remain in the Convention and another 9% said it should probably remain. Although the party consistently voted in favour of withdrawal, after the President decided to return the law to the Saeima for reconsideration, NA agreed to leave the final decision to the 15th Saeima. Advertisements NA explained this as a question of the timing of the vote rather than a change in its position. Nevertheless, it created a political risk of losing supporters from both camps. For NA’s more moderate and strongly pro-European voters, the very initiative to withdraw may have been unacceptable, while more firmly conservative voters could have viewed the compromise and postponement of the decision as insufficiently consistent. It should also be noted that a poll conducted by Latvijas Fakti in cooperation with Faktu logs between the 21st and the 31st of August showed support for NA at 7.3% of all respondents. While NA ranked fifth in the SKDS poll, it placed third in the Latvijas Fakti survey, where 23.1% of respondents remained undecided. However, the two polls are not directly comparable. SKDS and Latvijas Fakti use different methods to reach respondents, and such methodological differences can affect the results. Advertisements What is the bottom line? NA still has a recognisable ideology, experienced politicians, ministerial posts and a long-standing core electorate. However, its once clearly defined political niche has become crowded, while the values and positions that matter to nationally minded voters are increasingly being adopted by the party’s competitors within the same political space. On the more moderate side, NA faces competition for voters from Prime Minister Andris Kulbergs’ United List and, on certain issues, New Unity. ZZS, the New Conservative Party (JKP) and others are also competing for socially conservative, family-oriented voters. On the national-conservative side, there is also Rising Sun for Latvia (ASL), founded by Raivis Zeltīts after he left the National Alliance a year ago. ASL essentially offers the same ideology as NA, but in a much more radical form. ASL has little prospect of entering the 15th Saeima, but the roughly one percentage point of support it has attracted has most likely come at NA’s expense. Advertisements At this point, the main question is not whether NA will clear the 5% threshold required to enter the 15th Saeima. Both the SKDS and Latvijas Fakti ratings indicate that it will. The more important question is whether voters who care about the Latvian language, national security, a restrictive migration policy, demographics and a firm, critical stance towards Russia still regard the National Alliance as the principal political representative of those interests. It is precisely this political “ownership” of the national-conservative electorate that NA is now fighting to retain. Restoring some of their pre-2022 complex mutual interdependence through US mediation, even if only for the wintertime, could facilitate a series of pragmatic diplomatic-military compromises aimed at resolving the Ukrainian Conflict and jointly building the new continental security architecture. Zelensky recently proposed a partial truce with Russia that would include, among other things, eschewing attacks on each other’s energy infrastructure. The strategic context concerns Russia’s ramped-up systematic strike campaign against Ukrainian power plants, gas stations, ports, and most recently, locomotives, all of which aims to cripple its military logistics by winter for achieving a Russian breakthrough. The Kremlin therefore doesn’t have any interest in accepting this lopsided arrangement. That could change, however, if Russia makes at least the energy dimension of Zelensky’s proposal conditional on resuming its pipeline exports to Europe. It’s not just Ukraine that’s poised to experience its must difficult winter in years but the EU as a whole too according to the European Commissioner for Energy and Housing in a recent interview with the Financial Times. This is due to the global fuel crisis brought about by the Third Gulf War and Ukraine’s spree of attacks against Russian refineries this year. Ukraine desperately needs relief from Russia’s systematic strikes against its energy infrastructure this winter, the EU desperately needs more energy amidst the global fuel crisis during the same season, and Russia is unlikely to turn down the influx of revenue even if the windfall is only for several months. A deal could take the form of resuming gas exports to Germany via the one undamaged Nord Stream pipeline possibly together with oil and gas exports to Poland (and beyond) via the Druzhba and Yamal pipelines. The resumption of Russian pipeline exports to Europe, even if only for the winter, would restore some of their pre-2022 complex mutual interdependence for raising the odds that the energy truce is respected. The EU will still survive the winter even without Russian pipeline imports, and Russia can continue funding its military operations even without pipeline exports to Europe, but Ukraine might not survive without relief from Russia’s systematic strikes against its energy infrastructure. Accordingly, the EU could sever its imports from Russia if Russia violates the energy truce, while Russia could sever its exports to the EU if Ukraine does so instead. While skeptics might suspect that Russia has more to gain from violating the energy truce due to Ukraine’s increasingly desperate military-strategic situation, Russia has a greater interest in jointly building the new continental security architecture with European NATO (E-NATO), which it can’t do without a relative normalization of ties. All of this is sensible. If an energy truce is agreed to on the condition of Russia resuming at least its Nord Stream exports to Europe, then the “snowdrop diplomacy” formula proposed here could be advanced, which might see the mutual drawdown of E-NATO forces from the Baltic States in parallel with Russian ones from Belarus. The US might then purchase Nord Stream from Russia as has been floated, and perhaps also the Belarusian parts of Druzhba and/or Yamal, for upholding this new order and facilitating a grand deal over Ukraine. The resultant security architecture could have partial buffers in the Baltic States, Belarus, and Ukraine, while the western flank of the “ cordon sanitaire ” would have a US-backed Polish-led Intermarium counterbalance a German-dominated militarized EU . Poland would also still be the US’ LNG hub in Europe since the US would probably raise the price of the Russian pipeline gas under its control to keep its own gas competitive. This balance of interests is realistic and should thus be seriously considered. Subscribe to Post Comments 24 comments Even the idea that this is “sensible” doesn’t wash for me. There seems nothing for Russia in Korybko’s proposal beyond some airy-fairy idea of “normalization” being necessary as a prelude to a new European security architecture. The funding pool for the renovations, which Fire Chief Rick Cousins estimated at about $1 million, grew a bit Wednesday, with a $10,000 donation from Ron Clark Ford's Ron and Todd Clark. "It's just a good cause," said Todd Clark, noting the largely volunteer department is probably underfunded and under-recognized for the work they do. "We've got a lot of citizens and residents here locally volunteering, and we want to do what we can to help out," Clark said. The family also recently gave $10,000 to Pathways Health Centre for Children as part of an annual donation campaign, through the Sarnia Community Foundation. Key is improving safety for firefighters, Cousins said, thanking the Clarks for their generosity. "It means a great deal to us to know that you believe in and support the work we do in and around our community," he said. Currently, washing machines are in the open bay area at the station, not in a separate clean area, he said. "It's a major renovation for us . . . a major step in the right direction," Cousins said. The project also includes new washrooms, and makes use of the existing building, he said. Bunker gear decontamination is a standard component in any new fire station construction, he said. Before the donation, about $269,000 had been saved for the project, according to a June report to the Petrolia North Enniskillen fire committee. Article content Preliminary work, including building a ramp and replacing a water line, is currently underway, Cousins said. About $20,000 in window replacement and building exterior work was planned this year, the June report from Enniskillen Township clerk Christine Poland says. Final approval on the larger fire station renovation project is still pending, Cousins said, noting costs are expected to increase if it's delayed. The remainder of the cost is expected to come through municipal budget processes in 2027 and 2028, Poland's report says. Cousins said the fire service includes 25 firefighters, four captains, and two deputy chiefs. Between January and June, the service responded to 72 incidents, Cousins said, in a September update to Petrolia council.
